food.text: The Marajoara culture of Marajó island, at the mouth of the Amazon River, appears to have flourished between 800 AD and 1400 AD. Heavy tooth wear in human remains suggests a diet based mainly on seed crops, tree fruits, and fish. The Marajo peoples limited their consumption of starchy root crops like manioc.

When Europeans first encountered them, the Guarani were sedentary and agricultural, and are estimated to have numbered some 400,000 people. They subsisted largely on manioc, maize, wild game, and honey. Their early villages often consisted of communal houses called malocas, each holding several families under a chief.

The Indigenous peoples of Brazil were traditionally mostly semi-nomadic tribes. They subsisted on hunting, fishing, gathering, and migrant agriculture. When the Portuguese arrived in 1500, the Natives lived mainly on the coast and along the banks of major rivers.

Native Americans of the Amazon rain forest may have used terra preta to make the land suitable for large-scale agriculture. That farming could have supported large populations and complex chiefdoms. The Marajoara culture may have supported a population as large as 100,000 people.

The Tupinambá relied on agriculture for most of their resources, using the slash-and-burn technique. Both women and men worked the fields, with the women often tilling the soil before the men carried out their duties. They also hunted, fished, and gathered, though not to the extent of their farming.

Cassava was a staple food of pre-Columbian peoples in the Americas. Its wild ancestor is centered in west-central Brazil, where it was likely first domesticated no more than 10,000 years ago. Forms of the domesticated plant can still be found growing wild in the south of Brazil.

The Mapuche of south-central Chile and southwestern Argentina have a traditional economy based on agriculture. Their social organization consists of extended families under the direction of a lonko, or chief. In times of war they elected a toki, meaning axe-bearer, to lead them.

Stone griddles turned up during excavations at Teso Dos Bichos on Marajó island, but only very rarely. Their scarcity is taken as another marker of the absence of root crops from the diet at Marajo. The main agricultural tools there were stone axes.

Marajoara mounds housed malocas, Amazonian longhouses with several hearths lined up along the center, each likely serving one nuclear family. They had permanent cooking facilities made of baked clay and plastered floors that were frequently repaired. At places such as Os Camutins, up to 20 structures were built atop one another.

Cassava comes in sweet and bitter varieties, and both contain toxins, the bitter kind in much larger amounts. Its roots, peels and leaves are dangerous raw, because they contain compounds that release poisonous hydrogen cyanide. Improperly prepared cassava can cause acute cyanide poisoning, with vertigo, vomiting, partial paralysis, collapse and death, and it is linked to goiter and to konzo, a neurological disorder affecting the ability to walk that can be fatal. Even so, the crop is exceptionally drought-tolerant and grows productively on poor soil.

Chicken bones found by Chilean archaeologists on the Arauco Peninsula in south-central Chile were thought to date from between 1321 and 1407 AD. This initial report suggested a Polynesian pre-Columbian origin for them. A later report examining the same specimens reached a different conclusion.

art.text: On Marajó island at the mouth of the Amazon River, a culture flourished that Charles C. Mann suggests thrived between 800 AD and 1400 AD. Its large pottery was elaborately painted and incised with representations of plants and animals. These pieces gave the first evidence that a complex society had existed on Marajó.

Mapuche material culture is known for its textiles, one of their best-known arts. Researchers have found fabrics made with complex techniques and designs, dated between AD 1300 and 1350. These are among the oldest textile data in the far south of the continent.

The Acre geoglyphs in Brazil are excavated earth structures that some Indigenous groups call "earth tattoos". A charcoal sample from the Fazenda Colorada site was dated to AD 1244-1378, placing at least one of these earthworks in the Medieval era.

The people of Marajó made far more than plain vessels. Their artifacts included urns, jars, bottles, cups, figurines, large statues, pendants, ear and lip jewelry, whistles, spindle whorls, and ceramic miniatures of axes and hammers.

Marajoara art is a type of pottery made by Indigenous peoples on Marajó from about 400 to 1400 AD. Successive phases of occupation each had their own distinctive pottery style. One source describes this art as representing the origin of pottery in Brazil.

One of the best-known Marajoara forms is the globular urn, with painted and modeled decoration showing anthropomorphic figures (primates). Other urns combined painting, incisions, excisions and modeling to show human-like and animal figures. Some vases carried painted geometric patterns instead.

Mound building on Marajó points to large, complex settlements. Only such settlements were believed capable of projects as extensive as major earthworks. Together with the pottery, this suggests the island was home to a sophisticated society.

Archaeologists found early Mapuche-area textiles in several graveyards and sites. These include Pitrén Cemetery near Temuco and the Alboyanco site in the Biobío Region, both in Chile, and Rebolledo Arriba Cemetery in Neuquén Province, Argentina.

Geoglyphs dating between 0 and 1250 CE are part of the evidence for dense populations along the Amazon. Beyond them, these peoples left no lasting monuments, possibly because they built with wood, which rots in the humid climate, since stone was unavailable.

Marajó island has no source of suitable stone, so stone tools and objects were very rare there. The few stone pieces found suggest they were used as high-status items and gifts, or in craft production.

war.text: According to primarily European writers' accounts, the Tupi were divided into tribes that constantly warred with each other, and tried to capture enemies so they could kill them later in cannibalistic rituals. Warriors captured from other Tupi tribes were killed and eaten, because the Tupi believed this let them absorb and digest the captured warriors' strength. The Tupi were also documented eating the remains of dead relatives as a way of honoring them.

From 1438 to 1533, the Incas incorporated a large portion of western South America, using conquest and peaceful assimilation, among other methods. Most peoples accepted Inca rule as a fait accompli and acquiesced peacefully, but refusal to accept it resulted in military conquest. After a conquest, the local rulers were executed, and their children were taken to Cuzco to be indoctrinated into the Inca nobility. At its largest, the empire reached northwest Argentina and a large portion of modern-day Chile.

When the Portuguese arrived, the Tupi inhabited three quarters of Brazil's coast, in tribes of 300 to 2,000 people. Among them were the Tupiniquim, Tupinambá and Potiguara. Despite a common language, there was no unified Tupi identity.

For Tupi warriors, dying valiantly in battle was a great honor, even for prisoners. A captive could also show courage during the festivities leading up to the sacrifice, where he would be killed and eaten in a cannibalistic ritual. Hans Staden, a German captured by the Tupi in 1552, wrote that they carried him to their village and declared they would devour him at their next festivity.

The Tupinambá lived in communities that sustained a population of about 100 people. The size and strength of these communities made them infamous in combat, but left them with very few alliances. The Tupinambá originally helped the Portuguese enslave other native populations, but the Portuguese eventually started to go after the Tupinambá as well. It was in part because they had so few allies that the Portuguese were able to conquer them.

In times of war, the Mapuche of south-central Chile united in larger groupings. They elected a leader called a toki, a word meaning "axe" or "axe-bearer". In peacetime their social organization rested on extended families under a lonko, or chief.

The Tupi killed and ate only captives they saw as strong and brave. They feared that eating a weak warrior would make them absorb weakness. The captives were killed in cannibalistic rituals, which they believed passed the victims' strength on to those who ate them.

literature.text: The Mapuche had no writing system before the Spanish arrived, so their stories and knowledge lived in speech. The name of their language, Mapudungun, combines mapu, meaning land, and dungun, meaning speech. It can be read as the speech of the land.
Guarani mythology tells of Yvy marã e'ỹ, the land without evils. It is a paradise where there would be no hunger, wars or diseases. In Portuguese it is called terra sem males.

In Guarani legend, Kerana, the beautiful daughter of Marangatu, was captured by Tau, a spirit of evil. Their seven sons were cursed by the high goddess Arasy, and all but one were born as hideous monsters. Even when lesser gods were forgotten in some areas, these seven were generally kept alive in the spoken tradition.

In Mapuche mythology, Antu is the principal Pillan spirit and the most powerful Pillan, governing the other Pillans. He represents the Sun, light, wisdom and spirit. He is married to Kueyen, a Wangulen spirit who represents the moon.

The classical Tupi language, spoken by the Tupi people along Brazil's coast, had a word for a manioc drink: kawĩ, meaning manioc beer. The word appears in a description of how the sound /w/ is used in Old Tupi. It hints at how central manioc was to Tupi daily life.

According to Rosana Bond, author of História do Caminho de Peabiru, the Tupi-Guarani paradise would be a real island that the vast majority of Guaranis believe lies to the east, somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. Reaching it requires a state of perfection called aguyjé, a spiritual state. The island would not be visible to any mortal, and if it were, it would move far away, since only those in a state of perfection could enter.

science.text: Densely populated settlements developed in the Upper Xingu region from 1200 to 1600 CE. Ancient roads and bridges linked communities that were often surrounded by ditches or moats. The villages were pre-planned and featured circular plazas.

Amazonian soil is naturally low in fertility, yet Indigenous farmers enriched it by adding charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure. The result, called terra preta or "black earth", keeps its charcoal for thousands of years, binding and retaining minerals and nutrients.

At Kuhikugu, at the headwaters of the Xingu River, people built long horizontal monuments on the ground instead of pyramids. Their engineering was sophisticated enough for bridges that crossed large sections of river and moats for defensive purposes.

Kuhikugu encompasses over 20 sites, each of which could have supported over 5,000 people, and all of them follow a similar layout. The black earth surrounding the area indicates large scale agricultural activity.

A coal sample from the Fazenda Colorada site in Acre was analyzed by radiocarbon dating at the University of Helsinki. It gave a calibrated age of AD 1244-1378, after a 24-year correction for the Southern Hemisphere. The site is one of the Acre geoglyphs, excavated earth structures that some Indigenous groups call "earth tattoos".

politics.text: Marajoara society on Marajó island, at the mouth of the Amazon, may have developed social stratification and supported a population as large as 100,000 people. Amazonian peoples may have used terra preta to make land suitable for the large-scale agriculture needed to support complex social formations such as chiefdoms.

Mapuche families lived in extended family groups under the direction of a lonko, or chief. In times of war, the Mapuche would unite in larger groupings and elect a toki, meaning "axe" or "axe-bearer", to lead them.
In 1500, the Tupi population was estimated at 1 million people, nearly equal to the population of Portugal at the time. They inhabited 3/4 of all of Brazil's coast when the Portuguese first arrived.

In 1493 the papal bull inter caetera divided claims to the New World between Spain and Portugal. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas revised it and moved the dividing line further west, separating the Portuguese domain to the east from the Spanish domain to the west.

Troops of the Inca Empire are reported to have reached the Maule River and fought the Mapuche between the Maule and the Itata Rivers. Most modern scholars place the Inca southern border between Santiago and the Maipo River, or somewhere between Santiago and the Maule River, so the bulk of the Mapuche escaped Inca rule.

In April 1500, Brazil was claimed for Portugal on the arrival of the fleet commanded by Pedro Álvares Cabral. The Portuguese found stone-using natives divided into several tribes, many sharing the Tupi–Guarani language family, who fought among themselves. The article names tribal warfare and anthropophagy (cannibalism) among the reasons the Portuguese decided to Christianize the natives. The Europeans also brought measles, smallpox, tuberculosis, gonorrhea and influenza, which killed tens of thousands of indigenous people who had no immunity, and whole tribes were probably annihilated without ever meeting a European.

Contact with the Incas is thought to have been the first time the Mapuche met people with state-level organization. It gave them a collective awareness distinguishing them from the invaders, uniting them into loose geopolitical units despite their lack of state organization.

The Inca southern border in Chile was made of several zones. An inner, fully incorporated zone had mitimaes protected by a line of pukaras (fortresses), while an outer zone had Inca pukaras scattered among allied tribes. Historian José Bengoa places this outer zone between the Maipo and Maule Rivers.

On 26 January 1500, Spanish navigator Vicente Yáñez Pinzón reached the Cape of Santo Agostinho, in the current state of Pernambuco. It was the oldest confirmed European landing in Brazilian territory, but Pinzón was unable to claim the land because of the Treaty of Tordesillas.

According to traditional historiography, Central Chile had been under Inca rule for about 60 years when the Spanish arrived. Recent works suggest at least 130 years of Inca presence, while historian Osvaldo Silva posits remarkably short chronologies of direct Inca rule.

philosophy.text: Guarani belief imagines a paradise called Yvy marã e'ỹ, or in Portuguese terra sem males, meaning "land without evils." It is a mythical land where there would be no hunger, wars or diseases.

Mapuche religion has no formal leadership or organizational structure and shows much internal variation. Among its many deities and spirits, one of the most prominent is Ngünechen, who is sometimes equated with the Christian God.

For the Guarani, the land is not a divinity, but it is impregnated with all religious experience. Their migrations are linked to the sense of land, territory and social space. Because of the prophetic tone of spiritual leaders and the search for new lands, some ethnographers claimed all Guarani thinking was oriented around the land without evil.

Marajoara religion may have echoed Amazonian cosmology, which understands the universe to be gender divided, with men related to the sun and women to the moon. Marajo settlement patterns are aligned east-to-west, consistent with such a gender-divided universe.

Mapuche traditional religion features a pantheon of gods and goddesses. The Meli Küyen are the four moon spirits, and the Meli Wangülen are the four spirits of the stars. The wenu püllüam are ancestral spirits in the sky.

Ancestor worship may have been very important to the Marajoara. When significant individuals died, the flesh was cleared from their bones and the remains were placed in elaborately decorated urns, which were topped with a bowl or platter. The urns were buried in the floors of houses on the mounds that the Marajoarans also used for residence, so the dead stayed close to the living.

In Mapuche mythology, Antu is the most powerful Pillán and governs the other Pillans. He represents the Sun, as well as light, wisdom and spirit, in opposition to darkness and the physical world. He is married to Kueyen, a Wangulén spirit representing the moon.

The Mapuche stopped the Incan invasion forces at the end of the 15th century. Yet some symbols and aspects of Andean religion are present among the Mapuche and Huilliche, whose lands lay well beyond the Inca border. One hypothesis traces these shared features to an older origin in Tiwanaku.

The Guarani practiced a form of animistic pantheism. Cannibalism was practiced on captives. According to the Jesuit missionary Martin Dobrizhoffer, they practiced cannibalism at one point, perhaps as a funerary ritual, but later disposed of the dead in large jars placed inverted on the ground.
Wine or chicha is regularly poured for the ancestors in Mapuche religion. Scholars differ, however, on whether ancestors play a significant role in the tradition at all.

culture.text: The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó island at the mouth of the Amazon River in northern Brazil. Charles C. Mann suggests it thrived between 800 AD and 1400 AD. It may have developed social stratification and supported a population as large as 100,000 people.

From around 1,000 years ago, the Tupi people gradually occupied the Atlantic coast of Southeast Brazil after migrating southward from the Amazon rainforest. By 1500 their population was estimated at 1 million, nearly equal to that of Portugal at the time.

The classical Diaguita period was marked by advanced irrigation systems and by pottery painted in black, white and red. The Diaguitas were not a unified people but were politically fragmented into several chiefdoms.

Marajoara ceramics were made by Indigenous peoples on Marajó island between 400 and 1400 AD. Each successive phase of occupation had its own distinctive pottery style, and Samuel Lopes says this art represents the origin of pottery in Brazil.
The Tupi were adept agriculturalists. They grew cassava, maize, sweet potatoes, beans, peanuts, tobacco, squash and cotton, among many other crops.

Early Guarani villages often consisted of communal houses called malocas, or ocas, each holding several families under the leadership of a chief. The Guarani were sedentary and agricultural, living largely on manioc, maize, wild game and honey.

Mapuche textiles are among the best-known arts of the Mapuche. Fabrics made with complex techniques and designs, found at sites such as Pitrén Cemetery near Temuco in Chile, have been dated to AD 1300 to 1350.

Women appear prominently in Marajoara art, portrayed as creators and as lineage heroes or founders. Households were matrilocal, and women were important in producing food, though other evidence suggests they may have held a lower status than men.

The Tupi were divided into tribes of 300 to 2,000 people each, including the Tupiniquim, Tupinambá, Potiguara, Tabajara, Caeté, Tamoios and Temiminó. Although they spoke a common language, there was not a unified Tupi identity.

Hundreds of years before the Portuguese arrived, the Tupinambá are said to have migrated from the south coast of Brazil to the northern coast for better hunting and farming. They settled in communities of about 100 people, whose size and strength made them infamous in combat but left them with very few alliances. The Tupinambá first helped the Portuguese enslave other native populations, but the Portuguese eventually started to go after the Tupinambá as well, and that lack of allies was in part why the Portuguese were able to conquer them.

The Diaguita culture emerged around 1000 CE from the Las Ánimas complex, which developed between 800 and 1000 CE. That complex had itself replaced the earlier El Molle complex, which existed from 300 to 700 CE.

Marajó island is thought to have been occupied until shortly before the European conquest. That puts the abandonment of the island by the Marajoara around AD 1300, even though some researchers think the culture persisted into the colonial era.
